Phosphates : OCP saisit la justice fédérale américaine
items.description: Le groupe marocain a fait appel du jugement du 15 juillet, qui a validé la conclusion de l'USITC sur le préjudice matériel, condition sans laquelle les droits compensateurs de 2021 n'auraient pas pu s'appliquer. Après près de trois ans de renvois et de réexamens devant la Cour du commerce international, le contentieux américain sur les phosphates marocains change de juridiction. La cour d'appel fédérale des États-Unis a enregistré le 17 septembre, sous le numéro 26-2275, le recours d'OCP contre le jugement du 15 juillet. Ce jugement avait confirmé la seconde détermination de la Commission américaine du commerce international (USITC), selon laquelle les importations d'engrais phosphatés du Maroc et de Russie ont porté un préjudice matériel aux producteurs américains. L'appel ne vise pas le calcul des subventions reprochées à OCP par le département du Commerce, mais uniquement le volet du préjudice. Lors de l'enquête initiale, Washington avait fixé le taux compensateur du groupe à 19,97 %, dont 18,42 points liés aux droits d'exploitation des phosphates concédés par l'État marocain, assimilés à une fourniture de ressources en dessous d'une rémunération adéquate. Cette ordonnance ne pouvait toutefois entrer en vigueur qu'à la condition que l'USITC constate un préjudice. Sur le plan procédural, OCP a déposé son avis d'appel auprès de la Cour du commerce international le 14 septembre. La juridiction d'appel l'a reçu le lendemain, puis inscrit à son rôle. Le dossier ne contient pas encore les moyens du groupe : les comparutions et les premières pièces sont attendues le 1ᵉʳ octobre, et le mémoire d'OCP le 16 novembre. La procédure regroupe également Eurochem North America, Phosagro, International Raw Materials et Koch Fertilizer, face aux États-Unis, à Mosaic et à J.R. Simplot. Dans son jugement, le juge M. Miller Baker a estimé que le dossier administratif étayait suffisamment la position de l'USITC : les volumes cumulés venus des deux pays, proposés à des prix concurrentiels ou inférieurs, avaient comprimé les prix du marché américain de façon significative. OCP avait contesté l'analyse des réexpéditions entre destinations américaines, celle des ventes perdues et le poids attribué aux importations dans la baisse des prix. Il avait aussi invoqué d'autres facteurs, dont la météo défavorable de 2018 et 2019, le recul de la demande et certaines décisions de producteurs américains. Le juge a répondu que l'USITC avait examiné ces éléments, et que la démarche du groupe revenait à demander au tribunal de substituer sa propre pondération des preuves à celle de l'agence, ce que le contrôle juridictionnel n'autorise pas. L'affaire est née d'une requête déposée le 26 juin 2020 par Mosaic. Pour 2019, l'USITC avait chiffré à 835 millions de dollars la valeur des importations couvertes en provenance du Maroc et de la Russie, contre 148 millions pour les autres origines. En mars 2021, quatre commissaires sur cinq avaient retenu l'existence d'un préjudice, ce qui avait permis la publication des ordonnances le 7 avril. Une première contestation d'OCP avait ensuite conduit, en septembre 2023, à un renvoi devant l'USITC, la Cour jugeant mal étayée l'hypothèse selon laquelle des cargaisons pouvaient être redirigées d'une destination américaine vers une autre. Un second jugement, en avril 2025, avait demandé à la Commission de reprendre plusieurs points de son raisonnement, avant que sa conclusion, maintenue, soit validée en juillet 2026. Ce débat judiciaire reste distinct de la décision de la présidence américaine de suspendre temporairement la perception des droits. Le 29 juin, Donald Trump a déclaré une urgence liée à l'approvisionnement agricole et autorisé, pour huit mois au plus ou jusqu'à la levée de l'urgence, l'entrée des produits marocains visés par l'ordonnance sans droits compensateurs. La Maison Blanche a justifié la mesure par l'insuffisance de la production américaine de phosphate face à la demande intérieure, exportations déduites. Appliquée depuis le 8 juillet par le département du Commerce, cette dispense exonère les importateurs et exportateurs concernés des droits comme des dépôts estimatifs, mais laisse intacts l'ordonnance de 2021 et le contentieux sur son fondement. Un premier examen quinquennal de l'ordonnance a par ailleurs été ouvert en mars. Le 24 juillet, le département du Commerce a estimé à titre préliminaire que sa suppression risquerait de faire perdurer ou réapparaître des subventions compensables, tandis que l'USITC évalue séparément le risque d'un retour du préjudice industriel. items.title: Éthiopie : sept groupes armés forment une alliance pour renverser le gouvernement d’Abiy Ahmed
items.description: Sept groupes armes ethiopiens ont annonce le 20 septembre la formation d'une alliance destinee a renverser le gouvernement du Premier ministre Abiy Ahmed, reunissant notamment des mouvements qui avaient combattu dans des camps opposes lors de la guerre du Tigre. Baptisee « Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival », cette nouvelle coalition rassemble des organisations issues de plusieurs regions du pays, du Tigre, dans le nord, jusqu'a la region Somali, au sud. Elle comprend egalement des groupes originaires de l'Oromia, de l'Afar et du Benishangul-Gumuz. Parmi ses membres figurent le TPLF et l'Amhara Fano National Movement, une coalition de groupes armes de la region Amhara. Ces deux forces s'etaient affrontees pendant la guerre du Tigre, le Fano ayant alors combattu aux cotes des forces federales contre le TPLF. Le conflit, qui a pris fin avec l'accord de paix de 2022, avait fait des centaines de milliers de morts et ete marque par de graves violences a caractere ethnique. Depuis 2023, Fano est a son tour engage dans un conflit avec le gouvernement federal dans la region Amhara, un conflit qui a fait des milliers de morts. Une alliance aux interets divergents Dans leur declaration, les groupes membres de la nouvelle alliance accusent le gouvernement d'Abiy Ahmed de centraliser le pouvoir et de marginaliser les differentes regions du pays. Ils affirment vouloir assumer une « responsabilite historique » en renversant le gouvernement. La coalition rassemble toutefois des groupes dont les interets et les revendications divergent, certains etant encore en desaccord sur des questions territoriales ou politiques. Le gouvernement federal n'a pas immediatement reagi a l'annonce. Le mois dernier, apres des informations faisant etat d'une possible coalition entre groupes armes, un conseiller du Premier ministre avait estime qu'une telle alliance chercherait a « semer le chaos », mais ne serait pas en mesure de renverser le gouvernement federal. Les tensions persistent au Tigre La creation de cette alliance survient alors que les tensions se sont de nouveau accentuees entre Addis-Abeba et le TPLF. En mai, le mouvement tigreen a repris le controle de l'administration politique de la region, en violation de l'accord de paix de 2022, accusant le gouvernement federal de ne pas respecter ses engagements. L'armee ethiopienne a mene ces derniers mois plusieurs frappes de drones contre des forces tigreennes, selon les donnees du projet Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED). Le gouvernement n'a pas commente ces frappes. L'armee a toutefois affirme la semaine derniere que pres de 300 combattants tigreens s'etaient rendus. Cette nouvelle dynamique s'inscrit egalement sur fond de tensions avec l'erythree, que l'ethiopie accuse de soutenir plusieurs mouvements insurges, dont le TPLF et Fano. Asmara rejette ces accusations.

Les Américano-Camerounais Joel Hans Embiid et les Philadelphia 76ers peuvent-ils aller plus loin en playoffs NBA cette saison ?
items.description: © Yellowbet Les Philadelphia 76ers ont atteint les demi-finales de la Conférence Est la saison dernière après avoir terminé avec un bilan de 45 victoires pour 37 défaites. Leur parcours en playoffs s’est toutefois arrêté face aux New York Knicks, qui se sont imposés 4-0. Ce résultat donne à Philadelphia un objectif clair pour cette nouvelle saison : atteindre les finales de conférence. L’effectif possède suffisamment de talent pour y parvenir, même si beaucoup dépendra de la disponibilité de Joel Embiid. Les 76ers ont remporté leur série du premier tour contre Boston 4-3 après avoir été menés 3–1. Ils ont ensuite affronté une équipe des Knicks qui a mis en évidence les faiblesses de Philadelphia. Cette élimination sans concéder le moindre match a également soulevé des questions sur la capacité des 76ers à compter sur Embiid tout au long d'une longue campagne de playoffs. Embiid élève le plafond de Philadelphia Lorsqu’il est en bonne santé, Embiid offre à Philadelphia un scoreur d’élite et un défenseur intérieur de premier plan. Le septuple All-Star a affiché des moyennes de 26,9 points, 7,7 rebonds et 3,9 passes décisives en 38 matchs de saison régulière la saison dernière. Ses absences ont constitué un problème majeur. Embiid a manqué une grande partie de la saison et a fait son retour pendant la série contre Boston après avoir subi une appendicectomie. Il a ensuite été gêné par une entorse à la cheville et des douleurs à la hanche durant la série face aux Knicks. Philadelphia a besoin d’un Embiid en meilleure santé cette saison. Sa présence modifie la manière dont les adversaires défendent les 76ers et donne à l’équipe une option fiable dans le jeu placé. Le fait de pouvoir compter sur lui pendant les playoffs pourrait avoir un impact plus important sur les ambitions de Philadelphia que n’importe quel changement individuel dans l’effectif. Maxey et le reste de l’effectif Tyrese Maxey apporte aux 76ers un autre scoreur et créateur de haut niveau. Sa progression continue devrait réduire la pression exercée sur Embiid, qui ne devrait pas avoir à créer presque toutes les possessions importantes. Le reste de l’effectif aura également son importance. Philadelphia devra pouvoir compter sur une adresse régulière à trois points, sur des minutes solides de la part du banc et sur suffisamment de profondeur défensive pour tenir le rythme d’une série en sept matchs. La série contre les Knicks a montré ce qui peut se produire lorsque ces éléments ne fonctionnent pas ensemble. Philadelphia a eu du mal à suivre, avant de finalement perdre le quatrième match de 30 points. Pour aller plus loin en playoffs, Maxey et les joueurs qui entourent Embiid devront être réguliers lorsque les défenses concentreront leur attention sur le pivot. Les 76ers ne peuvent pas se permettre de longues séquences durant lesquelles leur attaque devient trop prévisible. Philadelphia peut-elle atteindre les finales de conférence ? Les 76ers ont déjà montré qu’ils étaient capables de remporter une série de playoffs difficile. Leur victoire 4-3 contre Boston la saison dernière les a obligés à revenir d’un déficit de 3-1, leur offrant une expérience précieuse avant une nouvelle campagne de postseason. Pour les fans qui suivent les matchs en livestream ou utilisent des betting apps in Cameroon , les perspectives de Philadelphia dépendront probablement en grande partie de l’état de santé d’Embiid. Sa disponibilité pourrait influencer les attentes autour de l’équipe plus que presque tout autre facteur. Une qualification pour les finales de conférence est envisageable si Embiid reste en bonne santé, si Maxey continue de progresser et si le reste de l’effectif répond présent pendant les playoffs. La saison dernière s’est terminée en demi-finales ; la prochaine étape consiste à trouver suffisamment de régularité pour franchir ce tour. items.title: FTSE Russell: It will attract international capital, broader investor participation – Market operators
items.description: By Peter Egwuatu As Nigeria returns to the frontier market today, market operators have expressed confidence that foreign capital into the country is expected to be enhanced following global visibility. Reacting to the return to frontier market, Fiona Ahimie , President Chartered Institute of Stockbrokers , CIS said : “ Nigeria’s return to frontier market status should, over time, be a positive development for foreign portfolio investment, as it restores the country’s visibility and eligibility within the FTSE Russell global index framework. However, the immediate impact should not be overstated. Reclassification does not automatically translate into a significant surge of foreign capital. Rather, it places Nigerian equities back on the radar of global frontier-market investors and gives index-tracking funds the opportunity to consider Nigerian stocks within their investment universe. This is particularly significant because Nigeria was moved to Unclassified status in 2023, largely due to challenges around foreign exchange liquidity and capital repatriation, which made it difficult for international investors to enter and exit the market efficiently. For the domestic market, the more meaningful benefits could emerge gradually through improved liquidity, broader investor participation and stronger valuations. Increased foreign participation could boost trading activity and potentially reduce the valuation discount attached to Nigerian equities, especially large and liquid stocks that are more accessible to international investors.” Nevertheless, she said : “ The reclassification should be regarded as a catalyst, not a cure-all. Sustained foreign inflows will ultimately depend on Nigeria’s ability to maintain adequate FX liquidity, facilitate the efficient repatriation of investment capital, ensure policy consistency, deepen the capital market and achieve greater macroeconomic stability. In other words, Frontier Market status reopens the door to international capital, but the quality of the investment environment will determine how many investors ultimately walk through it.” Commenting as well, Chairman, ASHON, Sehinde Adenagbe , said : “ The return to Frontier Market status is significant because it enhances the international visibility and credibility of the Nigerian capital market. It signals that some of the market-access concerns that previously limited Nigeria’s participation in global investment indices are being addressed. This could encourage international fund managers, institutional investors and research analysts to pay greater attention to Nigerian equities. Over time, increased visibility can improve price discovery, deepen market participation and strengthen the ability of Nigerian companies to attract international capital through the equities market. “More importantly, the development could strengthen Nigeria’s position within the global capital-market ecosystem. Greater foreign participation would potentially increase market liquidity, broaden the investor base and improve the efficiency of capital allocation. It could also encourage Nigerian listed companies to improve corporate governance, disclosure and investor-relations practices as they compete for international capital. However, the long-term significance will depend on whether Nigeria can sustain the reforms that underpin market accessibility, particularly FX liquidity, capital repatriation, regulatory predictability and macroeconomic stability. The reclassification therefore represents an important vote of confidence, but its full value will be realised only if the market can convert renewed global attention into sustained investment and deeper liquidity.” Commenting on the development, Temi Popoola, Group Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer noted, “Nigeria’s restoration to FTSE Russell’s Frontier Market status is an important recognition of the progress made in our capital market and the strengthening of the infrastructure that supports it. Reclassification, however, is not the destination, it is a gateway. It opens the door to greater international attention on Nigeria and the chance to translate that visibility into meaningful, long-term investment. The timing is particularly significant. We are seeing renewed interest from major Nigerian businesses in the capital market as a route to mobilise capital and broaden ownership. Our responsibility is to ensure that the market has the efficiency, accessibility and depth investors need to participate with confidence. At NGX Group, we remain focused on strengthening the connections between Nigerian enterprise and capital, at home, across Africa and around the world. The next chapter is about turning renewed global interest into greater capital formation, broader participation and a market that can play an even more significant role in financing Nigeria’s growth.” The post FTSE Russell: It will attract international capital, broader investor participation – Market operators appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: In My Dreams
items.description: Illustrations by Hélène Blanc W hen I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me. The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify. The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing. This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing. Accompanying this feeling of an expanding hole at the center of me was a sense that I was losing more and more of myself to it, like shoreline eroded by rising waters. To lose myself felt less like oblivion than instability. I observed in myself a new susceptibility to the opinions of others, and a new recklessness, as if some dark, decisive action might either quiet my doubts about my fundamental worth or end my longing once and for all. I recall one particularly dangerous, drunken night that had me well over the legal limit, both aware that I was getting into a car that could kill me and others, and also not believing that any of it mattered. The onset of my devolving well-being was strange and sudden, and seemed connected to childhood in some way I couldn’t understand. I hadn’t been a tortured child but rather placid, if introverted. My parents always said that I had been easy to keep happy. It sometimes seemed to me as if the hole I was experiencing was one where some piece of my childhood had once resided. My friends found my behavior disturbing. I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk. A caring young woman I was dating could take no more of my savage, ranting mood swings and persistent despair. She broke up with me over tea at the student union and implored me to seek help. I knew she was right. Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear. But exactly what sort of help I might need, I didn’t know. I confided my woes to a friend who’d grown up on a farm in Kentucky. He never missed Sunday Mass, and when I told him about the hole inside me, he pulled a copy of The Seven Storey Mountain from his bag and handed it to me. Thomas Merton, he said, had written about something similar . It was what had led him to leave the world and become a monk. I found deep resonance in the book’s harrowing account of Merton’s time at Cambridge and Columbia—the intense restlessness and emptiness, the disgust and torpor and despair. But Merton’s solution was theistic: a turn to God that I could only read as naive and distorting. I didn’t have any interest in God. Even the passages that approached the specificity of my own experience were charged with personification that read as anachronistic at best: The room was very quiet. It was rather dark, too. And as I lay in bed, in my weariness and pain and disgust, I felt for a moment the shadow of another visitor pass into the room. It was death, that came to stand by my bed. I kept my eyes closed, more out of apathy than anything else. But anyway, there was no need to open one’s eyes to see the visitor, to see death. Death is someone you see very clearly with eyes in the center of your heart: eyes that see not by reacting to light, but by reacting to a kind of a chill from within the marrow of your own life. I knew this experience: a central chill, a lightlessness connected to the doomed feeling of some ultimate end. But I resisted any characterization that departed from the fundamental sensation itself—of a growing hole inside me. For no reason I knew, I was convinced that remaining honest with myself about this basic fact was the only thing I could do to help myself. My parents were worried. They flew out to visit me at school and figure out what was wrong. Over a meal they prepared for me in a hotel room with a kitchen, I confided in them. There was a hole inside me that I needed to address, I said. They were understandably perplexed. My mother found me a psychiatrist, an avuncular Brit who was more interested in my sex life than my interior void, which I insisted was more real than he seemed willing to allow. But something important endured from the handful of sessions I had with him. A volume on the shelf over his left ear drew my fascination, and would soon fill weeks of my life: Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams . That book began a process in me, what I’ve often called “curiosity” when I’ve told this story, but which is probably better described as a form of relationship. The nightly tumult of disturbing dreams persisted, and even if I couldn’t be sure whether Freud was right about how to make sense of them, simply attempting to do so seemed to help. Paying attention made it easier to remember my dreams, and to remember more of them. In one, I was carefully drawing an empty circle on a page of the Quran that my grandparents had given me as a boy, a circle through which—impossibly—I could reach and touch cool water. I awoke with the feeling that the hole inside me might be leading to something better, however unknown. Even so, it wasn’t until I mentioned that I was interested in dreams to a teacher I admired that I started to keep a detailed nightly log. This teacher had done a great deal of dream-work, and suggested that I tie a pencil to my finger to remind me, in those brief moments of stirring between sleep cycles, to write down whatever fragments were stirring in hypnagogic consciousness. So I did. What resulted was a daily haul of interior riches. The vividness of my unadulterated hopes and sorrows, the unusual expansiveness and wonder I experienced by night, lived on in the often-paradoxical images I would recall throughout the day. My study of Freud led to a similar scouring of the work of other psychoanalysts—and, later, mystics such as Emanuel Swedenborg, Ibn Arabi, and Rabbi Nachman—for clues about what kind of sense to be making of my dreams. In my final year of college, I encountered, in a late work of Carl Jung’s, the advice to treat dreams as meaningful psychic events, a technique to facilitate what Jung called their “compensatory” function—balancing the biases and limitations of one’s conscious attitudes. I took this to mean treating a dream’s images as real in their own right. Whether doing so had any such balancing effect on me, I can’t be sure. But my persistent despair seemed to be dimming; the hole inside me felt different the more I was able to gaze patiently into it for whatever was coming through. The dream-work was paying dividends, though what exactly was paying them out, I had no clue. Illustration by Hélène Blanc I know how what I’m about to share is likely to come off; it isn’t the first time I’ve spoken it aloud. I started to dream of things that hadn’t happened yet , to “see” things at night that then appeared in my life during the day. One of the earliest and most startling of these uncanny doublings took place in my first year after college. I was living and working in a small town in the Tuscan countryside, without a phone, before the internet. I dreamed that a friend I knew in Paris showed up on my doorstep with skis on his back. Two days later, I awoke to the sound of my name being called from down in the piazza, outside my front window. I opened the worn balcony doors to find the very friend I’d dreamed of; he’d gotten my Italian address from a mutual friend and seen that the town I was living in wasn’t too far out of the way as he made the trip from Rome up to the city in the Alps where he planned to spend a few days skiing. I resisted speaking of what had happened, lest I be impelled to name whatever in me had seized my bewildered attention. The Tuscan episode was not the last time dream and day seemed to cross wires. Years later, I would dream of a terrorist attack on Manhattan two days before 9/11, and of a malign, cough-inducing fog slowly engulfing the world several weeks before the eruption of the coronavirus into my (and the world’s) awareness—improbable coincidences I struggled to accept as such. And yet, these visions became the occasion to doubt any picture of the universe that failed to make room for what could only be experienced as a kind of magic. If the prognosticating mode had been the only benefit to accrue from my attention to my dreams, I might not have been so diligent in my recordkeeping. After all, I wasn’t seeing stock prices or lottery numbers, the only rationale many might have accepted for my habit of destroying every good night’s rest. For at that point, I was waking up every 45 minutes to reach for the bedside pad on which I made notes about whatever was moving around inside me. But my night work was opening up creative vistas. One mentor, well-versed in working with the unconscious, suggested that it was enlarging the space of what she kept calling—despite my confusion about what she really meant by it—my psyche. [ Read: McNeal, a play by Ayad Akhtar ] Indeed, a growing spaciousness was now my sense of the interior core where the hole had opened up. The hole itself wasn’t gone, but it had changed character, less a wound now than an opening, though I couldn’t always tell the difference. And yet, the trajectory seemed to be shifting. That pliant, receptive brightness bearing the imprint of something more than just my name, the self, began to feel heightened, enlarged. I had learned that some cultures conceived of the self as containing two parts: a smaller, individual, daily self, and a larger, multiple, primordial one. This greater self, it was believed, was the one that dreamed. Something about this way of thinking felt more useful—and more reflective of my experience—than any of the latest studies in neuroscience I read about the physiological functions of dreams. Psyche : Greek for “soul.” Which felt like a more appropriate frame of reference—despite my continued resistance to the language of theism—for experiences that so evidently defied the materialist doctrines of my late-20th-century education. To privilege the Newtonian model of classical mechanics—one object pushing or pulling another, all the way down to the molecules that formed consciousness—over the actual data of my experience felt like intellectual laziness. I understood that others would see my willingness to abide more patiently in the mystery as irrational. My usage of the Greek term started to give way to its English corollary. The word soul seemed to make better sense of whatever was expanding inside me, a rising that was also a deepening, married to the uncanny knowing of what seemed like prognostication, and, more valuably, to a natural empathy for others. And in case this comes off as more altruistic than seems reasonable: Less blinded by myself, more porous to others, I found, too, that I was becoming a better writer. [ From the November 2024 issue: Jeffrey Goldberg, Ayad Akhtar, Robert Downey Jr., and Bartlett Sher on writing in the age of AI ] Soul was, for me then, a mode of being mostly experienced in images by night that shaped my understanding by day—for example, that a close friend was like the abandoned dog I dreamed he was, long neglected by his family, never allowed into the house; an image that helped me navigate his touchiness, providing readier access to the wellspring of loving loyalty that coursed beneath his habitual choler. I found in the use of soul a capaciousness that not only accounted for this richer relationship to others and the world—and to myself—but served as a bridge to deeper mystery, and to a new patience that allowed me to acclimate to it. There were other benefits, too. Just as the vital, vivid stuff of my brain’s nightlife enriched my being—to use a word that joined soul in the lexicon of descriptive terms of dubious provenance—so did my immersion in dream dross seem to feed my capacities with language. There was a stronger tether now between word and thing, a tether, paradoxically, that operated simultaneously in many directions and layers. The webbed, protean mode of associative thinking—one thing reaching for another, in opposing vectors at once—was less an effort than a reflex, more instinctive than the ordinal fixity of my usual habits of mind. Shakespeare, whom I’d long struggled to apprehend, now made easier sense, even as the experience of reading him felt like perpetual entry into undiscovered country, the phonetic expatiations, the dense semantic clusters, the sounds and images opening up more and more effortlessly into a particular state of absorptive flow, a pleasing emotional and intellectual static that I took to calling “linguistic space.” I started taking a yoga class on the Upper West Side. Our becalming teacher spent the better part of our weekly hour teaching us to meditate. Setting aside my irritation with her hushed and holy tones, I found myself growing more susceptible to her instructions. I could catch a gap between thoughts that felt curiously similar to a rich blankness that resulted from hours spent in linguistic space. The fixed point of focus on the breath sharpened my mind and filled it with something closer to light than thought. On my own, I began to sit—sometimes for hours—in this pregnant blankness, exhibiting a facility for what the yoga teacher called “practice” that I couldn’t explain. My weekly hour with that yoga teacher sparked an interest in meditation that led to weeks, and years, of working with other instructors of inner techniques. I learned to visualize and hold in memory shapes derived from Gnostic practices and colors derived from Sufi ones. Intoning Abulafia’s list of Hebrew names for God at the proper pitch and volume shook the bones in my ear and nerves along my neck. Calm was promised, and often followed, though I wondered whether this said more about my susceptibility to suggestion than the practices themselves. Sometimes what followed was stranger. Once, as I sat in a darkened room at dusk, observing the breath going in and out of me, I felt that breath begin to breathe itself. In the half shadows, with my eyes closed, a startling brightness waxed and waned with the movement of air. What was this light? I wondered. Was this just the room’s faint light filtering through my eyelids, brightening and dimming as my pupils dilated and contracted with each breath? If so, was this suggestion too? I would come to no definitive answer. The inner light continued to strobe. If it was all suggestion, I didn’t mind. It was getting me further than faith had. From Meister Eckhart I learned to recognize in my meditative blankness a silence clean of longing, one that, if I could remain in it, would release an astonishing vitality. Others I studied with found it strange that my interest in meditation would be piqued by dream-work and quickened by pentameter. They sometimes remarked that what I was up to resembled anthropology more than devotion. They were only partly right. To me, it was all a study in being, or soul, or spirit (the latest addition to my lexicon)—which is to say, an inquiry into the substance and nature of the interior life. My reading, too, reflected the scavenging of a magpie in search of material from which to build its nest: the Phaedrus and Patanjali and Mulla Sadra; Being and Time one month, Mathnawi the next. What exactly I thought I was doing was not a matter of concern as long as I kept to myself about it. What I’m compressing into paragraphs here took so much longer, of course, and was hardly as sequential as telling makes it sound. I kept at it for the reward of the work itself. I had experiences of rapture (and sorrow) so deep, of pleasures so unprecedented, it was sometimes hard to return to the dishes and the rent. But I had studied with a remarkable Vedic teacher who warned me about seeking states rather than the truth. “What is the truth?” I once asked him as we sauntered along a Tennessee creek. He pulled his orange robe tighter against a rising spring wind. He was too smart to oblige. “The truth is not like knowledge about that tree,” he said, pointing to a blooming magnolia. “Only the tree knows its truth.” I didn’t want to pretend I understood him. “You write stories,” he said. “Inside the story is a meaning that is the reason for it. Not words that carry it, but the wordless substance of its truth you take away.” Despite my customary reticence about such things, I had occasions to compare notes with fellow travelers. One evening, at a fundraising function downtown, I found myself sharing martinis with a physician whose lived-in eloquence about his Zen practice felt like an opening. I was not expecting the lesson in brain science he proceeded to impart: I’d become addicted, he said, to activating certain parts of my cerebral cortex. Like an addict—I flinched at that word—I was pulling on neurological switches, training my brain to release its own pleasure chemicals through a growing grab bag of inner tricks. Clearly he didn’t approve. I was too embarrassed to ask why, even as I recalled my teacher’s warning not to chase states, but rather to seek the wordless substance of truth. I resisted the physician’s account even as I couldn’t ignore the unease it stirred in me. Illustration by Hélène Blanc M y fellow traveler was right, at least as far as neuroscience went. Studies were beginning to show that meditation—a loose term for the various practices of inner focus I was involved with—activated and deactivated specific parts of the human brain. In the 1990s, the neuroscientist Andrew Newberg studied advanced Tibetan monks and Franciscan nuns as they entered deep meditative states . The results were strikingly similar. In both groups, areas of the brain believed to be responsible for orienting us in space and time showed markedly decreased activity, as if the neural basis for the boundary between self and other had gone quiet. They were using very different techniques, but the results, neurologically speaking, were nearly indistinguishable. Each group, however, described the experience differently: the nuns as a feeling of union with Christ, the monks as a state of emptiness. I knew enough about Buddhism to recognize in that word, emptiness , something very different from the hole that had opened up inside me during early adulthood. For the Buddhist, perception of the nature of reality discloses the identity of emptiness with form, and form with emptiness. It’s a perception described in other traditions by other means, and sometimes, in Christianity, as an annihilation of the individual personality in the presence of God. The maps and words and techniques were different; somehow, the underlying experience itself, beyond words or ideas, was the same. Not quite in the words of my Vedic teacher: The brain scans were a story containing a truth known only to the one inside them. F or a long time , all of this felt like little more than a motley, life-enhancing assortment, which is not to downplay the valuable place it had in my life. Rightly or wrongly, I attributed the return of my fundamental stability after the harrowing years of early adulthood—and the return of the placid, placable self I’d known much earlier in life—to my commitment to daily practice. I would come to think of inner work as an adult corollary to the joyous absorption of childhood play. I’d found a way to play again, I concluded, and somehow this had seemed to “fill” the hole again. But the life of the spirit was not what I took my real life to be. I was a writer. I wanted to know the broken world that was, not the healed one that could be. I had no fundamental interest in escaping the human condition. To the extent that spirit—or soulfulness—anchored my curiosity, quickened my perceptions, deepened my empathy, I rationalized its creative and analytical utility. In truth, something less tangible than optimization bound me to practice. It kept me in the company of more eternal conundrums, questions of consciousness and origin and meaning for which, of course, I expected no answer. But proximity to the unknown—living contact with it, if you will—seemed like a worthy form of knowledge. In this, I was like many friends who took psychedelics; I wanted to recover the awe and mystery I recognized in their accounts when they shared them. For the most part, though, I was still doing what my teacher had warned me against—chasing states. In part, this was a function of resisting meaning. I had been too respectful of my teacher back then to tell him I wasn’t sure that a story’s meaning mattered to me the way he assumed it would. But I felt the slow accretion of a wordless substance inside me, not well-being or certainty or the rapture of some fugitive sublime, but something I might call intimacy: intimacy with an inwardness spied only indirectly, whose purer acquaintance I seemed to be making very slowly indeed. With the hindsight of decades, I can track a tectonic shift away from the visible to something more diffuse and sustaining, an interior through line that has both warned me against the tyranny of acquisition—of things, of states—and provided the means of finding sustenance in absence. Whatever this is, whatever name I might give it, I can’t deny that it all seems to have proceeded from that perception of a hole I felt or imagined when I was younger. William James might have called it a “sick soul”; I still don’t feel entirely confident about what word to use for the continuity that I’ve found or constructed, though some word has always been necessary. I had spent years resisting every vocabulary that exceeded the raw data of sensation, only to find that this austerity, too, had to be exceeded. Too much of what mattered most in my own life had remained unspoken not because it was unreal, but because I did not know how to bring it into language without betraying it. For decades, I steered conversations away from these inner experiences, obedient to the rule that such things could not be talked about without sounding foolish or deranged. But my reticence began to feel like capitulation to falseness. It took me years to understand that my silence was not only protective but deforming—for without others to hear it, the still, small voice within was so much harder to discern. And yet, the silence was not my own to break. With so little room in our common life for such things, we have no common language for them either. Ralph Waldo Emerson knew the problem. In “ The Over-Soul ,” he wrote that language could not paint this “subtile” order of our experience in its own colors; but he knew how important it was to keep trying. The great Russian novelists knew it too, treating soul not as a word reserved for Sundays, but as the moral substance of life. I’ve found myself mourning not their metaphysics but their seriousness, their acceptance of the inscrutable boundlessness of the inner life—unruly, morally consequent—as a subject for public speech. What matters to me now is less the defense of any particular term than the search for a language in which such things can be spoken of seriously, in fiction and elsewhere, without piety or diagnosis. Without a language for speaking openly together about the inner life, what often matters most to us remains locked away, inaccessible to the inquiry and challenge vital to all knowledge. As I finished a draft of this essay, I had a dream. In it, I stood at the edge of a well—another hole, I realized as I made note the following morning—where there was no bucket to draw water. Around it moved countless people in a flurried hubbub, shepherds and masons and architects, all of us trying to figure out how to draw the water whose surface we could see in the faint shimmering at the bottom. It was going to take time, I thought, before we figured it out—just as I awoke. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “In My Dreams.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. items.title: In Defense of Guilt by Association
items.description: J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed have very little in common ideologically and seem to like each other even less. As part of a nasty exchange of personal insults last month, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan implied that Vance’s grandfather would disapprove of the vice president’s Indian American wife. In response , Vance called El-Sayed “very, very evil” and warned him to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth because she’s way out of your league.” Yet even as Vance and El-Sayed are happy to trade schoolyard taunts, they can agree on at least one thing: that guilt by association is a contemptible means of scoring cheap political points. “I’m tired of this guilt-by-association thing,” El-Sayed complained earlier this year, when he was asked about his decision to campaign alongside Hasan Piker, an internet shock jock who has said that “America deserved 9/11,” described allegations of sexual violence on October 7 as “rape fantasies,” and praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of the world,” among many other charming bon mots. Despite repeated calls from within his own party to renounce Piker, El-Sayed refuses to do so. Vance is facing a similar situation with his friend Tucker Carlson. Vance “ doesn’t believe in guilt-by-association cancel culture ,” a spokesperson said in September 2024, after the then-senator appeared onstage with the conservative podcast host. In the years since his firing from Fox News, Carlson has lauded a Holocaust denier as “the most important historian in the United States,” accused a small Jewish sect of orchestrating the war in Iran, and praised Vladimir Putin as “the most effective leader in my lifetime.” Carlson, whose show returns again and again to the supposed perfidy of the Jews, has become the country’s highest-profile promoter of anti-Semitism. He recently held a friendly conversation with a guest who claimed that algebra was “fake math” created for “goy slaves.” Vance was asked directly about his relationship with Carlson at a White House press conference earlier this month. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go.” [ Jonathan Chait: J. D. Vance’s disingenuous defense of Tucker Carlson ] El-Sayed and Vance would have us believe that their troublesome friends are no different from the people in our own lives whose political views we abhor but whom we nonetheless love and appreciate. “If I had to choose between betraying my country and betraying my friend, I hope I should have the guts to betray my country,” the English writer E. M. Forster wrote in 1938 as Europe hurtled toward war. It’s a noble sentiment, a paean to friendship over tribe. But Piker and Carlson are not the equivalent of your crazy uncle. And El-Sayed and Vance are not regular citizens; they’re political figures whose judgment and choices affect other Americans’ lives. One’s choice of friends is in fact an excellent sign of character, and in this respect, both Vance and El-Sayed have demonstrated a conspicuous lack of it. The tactic known as “guilt by association” evokes the legacy of Senator Joe McCarthy, whose feral zeal for exposing Communists, real or imagined, was so era-defining that it inspired the attachment of an ism to his surname. McCarthy’s sin wasn’t his anti-communism, however—there were indeed highly placed Soviet agents in the federal government. It was his recklessness and lack of concern for the truth. There has to be a reasonable middle ground between conducting a witch hunt and blatantly ignoring someone’s willingness to fraternize with genuinely disreputable people. Now that their associations are in the spotlight, El-Sayed, Vance, and their respective ideological compatriots are eager to minimize them. In a softball interview with Piker several months ago, the Pod Save Americ a host Jon Favreau, a prominent liberal opinion-shaper, said that he wants Democrats to take the “Don’t Talk About Hasan Piker For A Day Challenge.” Asked about Piker’s remarks concerning 9/11, El-Sayed tried to depict himself as a victim of the “cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring back.” A “Vance ally” echoed a similar sentiment to The Washington Post about the vice president’s relationship with Carlson, saying , “We’re done with the canceling, period.” No one should accept these evasions. In April, El-Sayed deployed Piker to boost support among young voters at Michigan State and the University of Michigan. In the final hours before polls closed, El-Sayed appeared at a pool party with Piker and other internet influencers in Detroit. Vance’s association with Carlson goes much deeper. In a 2021 interview recalling the time they first met, Vance described their immediate recognition of each other as “the guy who’s exactly right about what’s going on in the country.” Carlson helped persuade Donald Trump to select Vance as his running mate; Vance hired Carlson’s son as his deputy press secretary. When Vance guest-hosted Charlie Kirk’s show after the conservative activist’s assassination, one of the first people he invited into the vice-presidential suite was Carlson. (At Kirk’s funeral six days later, Carlson delivered a eulogy that seemed to imply that the Jews had murdered Kirk just as they had Jesus Christ.) The most obvious reason El-Sayed and Vance haven’t disowned their noxious friends is that both Piker and Carlson command large audiences. Politics is about winning votes, and a moral miscreant’s is worth the same as a saint’s. Other politicians have done much worse than associate with the likes of Piker and Carlson. What’s more troubling is that El-Sayed and Vance each appear to sympathize with at least some of what their influencer friend espouses. On multiple occasions, Vance has shown that he either doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about anti-Semitism. He once dismissed outrage over a group of Young Republicans joking about gas chambers as “pearl clutching” and characterized attempts to sideline bigots from the conservative movement as “endless, self-defeating purity tests.” One might think that Carlson’s frequent attacks on Vance’s boss, up to and including that Trump “ should be removed from office immediately ,” would have persuaded Vance, purely out of his own self-interest, to disavow Carlson. That he hasn’t done so indicates the high value he places on his association with him. If not for such data points, Vance’s friendship with Carlson would be easy to dismiss as misplaced affection for someone who helped advance his career. But Vance is on the record stating otherwise. Late last year, he said, I find the idea that Tucker Carlson—who has one of the largest podcasts in the world, who has millions of listeners, who supported Donald Trump in the 2024 election, who supported me in the 2024 election—the idea that his views are somehow completely anathema to conservatism, that he has no place in the conservative movement, is frankly absurd. This implies that Holocaust denial, claims of Jewish disloyalty to the United States, veneration of Putin, and a host of other poisonous ideas are welcome in the conservative movement. Even the white-nationalist influencer Nick Fuentes is fed up with Vance’s disingenuousness. “JD Vance panders to the far right but simply doesn’t want the baggage of associating with the far right,” Fuentes told The New York Times . “If he has a problem with ‘antisemites,’ then he should start by disavowing his best friend Tucker Carlson.” [ Read: The Hasan Piker question ] A similar ideological affinity appears to exist between Piker and El-Sayed, whose past statements on 9/11 and terrorism more broadly have a way of creating a moral equivalency between the United States and its Islamist enemies. “Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith,” El-Sayed tweeted five years ago on the 20th anniversary of the attacks. “Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country.” Earlier this year, after a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist rammed his car into a Detroit-area synagogue where 140 preschool-age Jewish children were playing, El-Sayed said that “hurt people hurt people,” a reference to the fact that the attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli air strike. (In a clumsy attempt at an apology, El-Sayed stubbornly refused to acknowledge the odious logic of his remarks, allowing only that he had chosen to administer “the right medicine at the wrong time.”) Like Prince Hal banishing Falstaff from the royal court , sometimes ending a friendship is a sign of the maturity necessary to lead. Barack Obama made just such a choice in 2008 after the hateful and conspiratorial remarks of his longtime pastor, Jeremiah Wright, were exposed to the world. Obama’s relationship with Wright was much more intimate than that between El-Sayed and Piker or Vance and Carlson; he had sat in Wright’s pews for decades, and Wright had baptized his children. And yet Obama ultimately turned his back on Wright, saying that the preacher’s divisive, anti-American “rants” were “an insult to what we’ve been trying to do in this campaign.” Obama understood that as long as he was associated with a character like Wright, he could never be a credible advocate for the national unity he claimed to seek. J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed each face a much easier decision—and each has failed to make the right one. It’s a testament to Americans’ increasing tolerance for extremism that both men seem to be getting away with it.

items.title: US media outlets to sue Trump administration after White House ban
items.description: MS NOW , CNN and Politico said on Monday they were suing the Trump Administration to protect their First Amendment rights after President Donald Trump’s announcement that he would ban the news outlets from the White House’s building grounds. The three news organisations said they had notified the government that they were filing their lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon as this week. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference,” they wrote in a joint statement. The lawsuit aims “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” they added. Representatives for the White House did not respond to a request for comment. Trump defended the ban in another social media post on Monday after the lawsuit was announced, calling the news media a security threat, without providing any evidence. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,” he wrote. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” The Trump administration has upended decades of tradition in dealings between the White House and press, denying the access many major news organisations have had to the president while elevating new media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He has also filed a number of lawsuits against news organisations. Trump’s latest move comes as his fellow Republicans seek to defend their narrow majorities in Congress in the November midterm elections as polls show the public souring on Republicans and Trump’s own approval ratings stand near historic lows. On Saturday, all three outlets said their journalists were turned away from the White House grounds and their press credentials confiscated, a day after Trump initially announced his ban in a social media post and threatened to block other outlets. He later addressed what he called his “ban on the free press” with reporters at an event in the Oval Office and said there was no particular incident that provoked the move. Asked what other news organisations could be targeted, Trump cited The New York Times and The Washington Post as “fake news” but said they had not been removed yet. The Associated Press , the White House Correspondents’ Association and others have criticised Trump’s ban, citing the fundamental American right to free speech and calling for access to be immediately restored. The Associated Press filed its own lawsuit after being barred along with Reuters last year from the group of reporters that cover the president’s daily movements.

items.title: US father explains decision to forgive wife who killed their three children
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of US mother Lindsay Clancy, has explained why he forgave her after she was accused of killing their three children, saying he feared he would have been “eaten up inside forever” if he had not reached that point. Speaking in an interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes, Patrick said he believed Lindsay’s severe mental illness played a role in the deaths of their children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. Lindsay, 36, has not disputed that she killed the children, while her defence team argued that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible. Her murder trial ended in a mistrial earlier this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. Prosecutors have yet to announce whether they will seek a retrial. Patrick said his decision to forgive Lindsay came partly in response to the way she was being described publicly. ‘I saw headlines that said, you know, “Killer Mom”, “Baby Murderer”, and “Monster”.’ And none of them were accurate,” he said. “I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn’t get there, I would be eaten up inside forever.” Patrick said Lindsay never asked him for forgiveness, but he chose to forgive her. “No. But I gave it to her,” he said when asked whether she had ever sought his forgiveness. The couple’s three children died in January 2023 after prosecutors alleged that Lindsay strangled them at their home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, before jumping from a second-floor window in an apparent suicide attempt. Patrick said he had noticed his wife’s mental health deteriorating months before the tragedy but did not know how to manage postpartum illness. “I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness. I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive. So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see,” he said. He also rejected suggestions that he had failed his family in the period leading up to the killings. “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day,” Patrick said. Patrick recalled the devastating aftermath of the tragedy, including the death of his youngest child, Callan, who survived for four days after being taken to hospital. “I got to hold him. I got to lie down next to him. And he died in my arms,” he said. The grief became so overwhelming that Patrick said he experienced suicidal thoughts. “There was a time when I didn’t think I would live to see my 35th birthday. And I was completely fine with it,” he said. He later moved from Duxbury to New York City, saying he needed anonymity and a place where he could grieve away from the intense attention surrounding the case. The tragedy has also been followed by intense online speculation about Patrick, including accusations that he was somehow responsible for his children’s deaths. Patrick described the speculation as deeply harmful, saying it distracted from what he believes should be the central issue: perinatal mental health. “It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health. And it’s done real harm to real people, myself included but also others,” he said. He also said the online attacks had affected his ability to appear in public. “It’s painful to see. And it makes it difficult to be in public,” Patrick said. Lindsay’s defence argued during the trial that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when the children died. The case remains unresolved following the mistrial, with Lindsay still being held in a psychiatric hospital while prosecutors decide whether to pursue another trial. Patrick has since remarried Dr Rachel Danis, and the couple are starting a family. He said he intends to ensure that his future children know about their late siblings. “I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they’re all your kids. And I can’t wait to tell them about their brothers and sister,” he said. The post US father explains decision to forgive wife who killed their three children appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: JI chief questions train delay as march comes to a pause at Sukkur
items.description: HYDERABAD: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Monday said it was time Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif put his foot down and withdrew the petroleum levy to provide “much-needed relief” to people, while questioning the delay in the train scheduled to take the party’s march towards Multan. The JI launched a protest “march” towards Islamabad on Sunday, departing Karachi by train and reaching Sukkur at night. Rehman had warned that if the government failed to abolish the petroleum levy, the protest could turn into one to oust the government. The march reached Sukkur on Sunday night by Rehman Baba Express, from where it was to head towards Multan via Shalimar Express. However, there was a four-hour delay in the train’s expected arrival at Sukkur on Monday, which the JI chief questioned at a press conference. “Does this delay have anything to do with our train march? Shalimar Express, which is not only a popular train but has been privatised, is delayed by four hours today,” he said. “If this delay in its [Shalimar Express] is a usual delay, then the federal government should explain the performance of Pakistan Railways,” Rehman said. He added that if a delay of four to five hours and its impact on the entire railway system were normal, then the government’s performance was for everyone to see. According to an official at Karachi’s chief controller office, Shalimar Express reached Karachi late, at 7:20am, thereby delaying its departure back to Hyderabad. The official attributed the late arrival to a fault in the engine developed in Sanghar district’s Tando Adam. Consequently, it reached Hyderabad at 1:25pm rather than the usual arrival time of 9:20am, delaying its expected time of arrival at Sukkur’s Rohri railway station, where Rehman’s caravan was waiting for it. The train march plans to reach Multan via Shalimar Express, and then the JI would march by road towards Islamabad. Addressing the media, the JI chief again termed the relief provided under the government’s scheme as insufficient, demanding that the petrol price be reduced. “The government has earmarked Rs26 billion per month in this head for offering subsidised fuel to motorcyclists. We feel that even this Rs26bn will not be utilised because not all the motorbikes are registered, whereas the government is recovering Rs150bn in terms of petroleum levy per month from people,” he added. Rehman also criticised the PPP, saying that while it claimed to support the JI’s campaign against the federal government, obstacles were allegedly being placed in the way of the train march and people seeking to welcome it.

items.title: Pakistan carries out 'calibrated’ airstrikes against terrorist targets in border region with Afghanistan
items.description: Pakistan conducted airstrikes on terrorist sites “in the border region with Afghanistan”, killing more than 28 terrorists, the information ministry said on Monday. In a statement, the ministry stressed that the “calibrated” strikes were carried out “against the hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations responsible” for the recent multiple terrorist incidents in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “Based on credible intelligence, selective targeting of terrorist camps and hideouts belonging to Fitna al Khawarij and its affiliates has also been carried out in the border region with Afghanistan with precision and accuracy,” the statement said. It added: “Three targets were destroyed with precision, including a suicide bombers’ training markaz (centre), killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. “Large quantities of weapons and ammunition stored at these marakiz (centres) and hideouts were also destroyed.” The state uses the term Fitna al Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). Prior to the airstrikes, security forces conducted a “well-planned intelligence-based ground operation” on Sunday against a group of terrorists in KP’s Kohat and Hangu districts, the ministry said. “As a result of precise and skilful engagement, nine khawarij belonging to Indian proxy Fitna al Khawarij were sent to hell, while several were injured,” the statement added. The ministry highlighted that Pakistan had “always strived for the maintenance of peace and stability in the region”. “However, the safety and security of our citizens remains our foremost priority. It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” it said, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. “In this context, our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs. Maximum precautions were taken, and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs,” the ministry asserted. The airstrikes come a few days after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar was in Kohat on Monday where he visited to the house of a police official martyred in the attack, according to state broadcaster Radio Pakistan . Speaking to the media in Kohat, he said he had also visited the injured personnel at the Combined Military Hospital. He added he was hopeful that terrorism would be eradicated from the country after meeting the heirs of the martyrs and ghazis. “We will not rest until eradicate terrorism from its roots,” he asserted. There has been a resurgence in terrorism in Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021. On Sunday, two officers and four others were martyred while eight terrorists were eliminated during a fire exchange between a security forces convoy and armed combatants, the military’s media wing said. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from Dec 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA). ‘Ghazab lil Haq under vision Azm-i-Istehkam’ In its Monday statement, the information ministry reaffirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign Ghazab lil Haq under vision ‘ Azm-i-Istehkam ’ by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and -supported terrorism from the country”. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. The last time Pakistan carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan was in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . According to Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had also carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. Last week, responding to Afghan Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid’s remarks , the information ministry had stressed that Pakistan consistently pursued constructive engagement with the Afghan Taliban, but would not allow what it called the “pretence of dialogue” to shield those threatening its people. In his remarks, Mujahid had said Kabul wanted dialogue with Islamabad, but had also warned of “retaliatory action” if Pakistan carried out military operations inside Afghanistan — a warning that the information ministry rejected.

items.title: Pakistan, EU sign financing agreements worth €65m
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and the European Union (EU) on Monday signed €65 million (about $75m) in financing agreements to support global gateway investments, strengthen the rule of law and business environment and enhance energy and environmental resilience. The agreements were signed by the EU Ambassador to Pakistan Raimundas Karoblis and the secretary of the Economic Affairs Division (EAD), Muhammad Humair Karim, on behalf of their respective sides, the division said in a statement. Under the agreements, the EU is to provide a total of €65m (about Rs20.64bn) to launch three separate programmes: Global Gateway Development Facilitation for Pakistan, Energy and Natural Environment Resilience in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and EU Support to the Rule of Law and Business Environment in Pakistan. Funded under the EU’s Multiannual Indicative Programme 2021-2027, the initiatives focus on three main aspects of Pakistan’s development. The first, Global Gateway Development Facilitation for Pakistan, envisages investment management and financial enablement of environmental projects to attract more foreign investment to the country by improving the tax system and strengthening the government’s long-term financial planning. The second project, Energy and Natural Environment Resilience in KP, is designed to expand renewable energy in rural communities that are not connected to the electricity grid. It will also provide training to help attract private investment and increase private sector involvement in KP’s energy sector. The third programme, building on previous EU assistance, covers EU support to the rule of law and business environment in Pakistan to help people access the police, prosecution, courts and legal aid in the provinces of KP and Balochistan. The programme will also support Punjab and Sindh in expanding the use of alternative and commercial dispute resolution mechanisms in legal cases, in order to build interest from European and other companies in investing in these provinces. The EAD said the EU’s development cooperation with Pakistan remained focused on economic development, climate resilience, governance and the rule of law, as well as human rights and sustainable natural resources. Speaking on the occasion, EAD Secretary Karim expressed his appreciation for the EU’s continued support and partnership. He highlighted the timely nature of the interventions, highlighting its strong relevance to Pakistan’s goals of increased foreign investment, improved access to electricity in off-grid rural areas in KP, and advanced standards in the rule of law and the resolution of commercial disputes. Ambassador Karoblis said the agreements demonstrated the EU’s commitment to supporting Pakistan’s economic development and investment ambitions under the flagship Global Gateway initiative. He noted that they would also support the authorities in KP to build a stronger and resilient energy sector, while promoting the sustainable management of natural resources. “The rule of law will further strengthen access to justice for citizens in KP and Balochistan,” he said. “In addition, Punjab and Sindh will benefit from our support to strengthen alternative and commercial dispute resolution through collaboration with the judiciary, legal professionals, universities and the business community.”

items.title: Lutte TV Awards 2026 : Sa Thiès sacré meilleur lutteur, Baye Ndiaye meilleur promoteur
items.description: La 3e édition des « Lutte Tv Awards », organisée le samedi dernier à Dakar par Lutte Tv et son partenaire Éric Favre, a consacré les principaux acteurs de la saison 2025-2026. Sa Thiès a ainsi été élu meilleur lutteur avec frappe, Ordinateur, celui de la lutte sans frappe, Petit Lô meilleur espoir, Modou Lô distingué pour son fair-play et Baye Ndiaye encore sacré meilleur promoteur. Les principales composantes de la lutte se sont retrouvées, le samedi 19 septembre, à l’hôtel Noom de Dakar, à l’occasion de la troisième édition des Lutte Tv Awards. Une cérémonie organisée par Ibrahima Faye, dit « Beuz », et son partenaire Éric Favre, qui a réuni plusieurs personnalités de haut prestige de l’arène. Dans la catégorie du meilleur lutteur de lutte avec frappe, Sa Thiès a été distingué par les votants. Le pensionnaire de l’école Balla Gaye, vainqueur de Modou Lô de Rock Énergie, le 5 avril 2026, succède ainsi à Franc de Jambars, deuxième du classement cette année. La distinction, dotée du titre « Yékini », ancien « Roi des arènes », récompense la belle saison du cadet de Balla Gaye 2, qui est devenu « Roi des arènes » à la suite de son succès sur le « Roc » des Parcelles assainies. Franc s’est classé deuxième après sa prestation face à Tapha Tine de Baol Mbollo, le 15 février 2026. Ada Fass de Fass-Benno complète le podium, après sa victoire sur Eumeu Sène de l’écurie Tay Shinger, le 19 avril 2026. Dans la catégorie du meilleur lutteur sans frappe, dotée du titre « Reug Reug », Ordinateur de l’école Boy Niang s’est imposé. Il succède à Ngagne Sène, classé deuxième, devant Siny Sembène, dit « Siny Bargny », troisième. Modou Lô, le fair-play récompensé Chez les meilleurs espoirs, Petit Lô de Rock Énergie, neveu de Modou Lô, a été sacré. Il succède à Bébé Gouye Gui, lauréat de la précédente édition. Bébé Oufly de Rufisque a créé la surprise en prenant la deuxième place, devant Fils de Bm de l’école Bada Dione. Chez les promoteurs, Baye Ndiaye reste maître du jeu. Le patron d’Albourakh Events a été élu meilleur promoteur de lutte avec frappe pour la troisième fois consécutive. La distinction de cette année porte le nom de Gaston Mbengue. Mansour Bâ de Jambaar Productions s’est classé encore deuxième, devant Makane Mbengue de Gaston Productions. Pour le prix du lutteur le plus fair-play, Modou Lô a été distingué. L’ancien « Roi des arènes » devance Lac de Guiers 2 de l’écurie Walo, deuxième, et son coéquipier Alioune Sèye 2, troisième. La distinction porte le nom de l’ancien lutteur Mor Fadam. La catégorie du meilleur chroniqueur, dotée du titre de feu Birahim Ndiaye, ancien lutteur et chroniqueur, a également livré son verdict. Abo Fiw a créé la sensation en détrônant Fadam 2, lauréat de la précédente édition. Ce dernier se classe deuxième, devant Modou Anta « Sans Frontières » de Gaston Productions. Les organisateurs ont également procédé à d’autres distinctions. Baye Balla Mboup de Bantamba Tv a ainsi été « désigné » meilleur reporter de lutte de la saison 2025-2026, tandis que Lambalogue a reçu le titre de « Meilleur influenceur ». À préciser que, pour ces deux dernières distinctions, il n’y a pas eu véritablement de vote. Face aux plaintes de Baye Balla Mboup et de Lambalogue, chacun se réclamant meilleur dans sa catégorie, Ibrahima Faye, dit « Beuz », a expliqué que les organisateurs avaient « improvisé » ces distinctions afin de les honorer, estimant qu’ils les méritaient également. Plusieurs figures de proue de la lutte ont honoré la cérémonie de leur présence. Parmi elles figuraient Bira Sène, président de la Fédération sénégalaise de lutte, Malick Ngom, ancien président du Comité national de gestion de la lutte, Gris Bordeaux, président de l’Association des lutteurs, et Yakhya Diop, dit « Yékini », ancien « Roi des arènes ». La soirée a également été marquée par une animation musicale assurée par le chanteur Sidy Diop. Les invités ont pu profiter d’un moment de convivialité autour de mets et de grillades servis à l’occasion. Par Abdoulaye DEMBÉLÉ

items.title: La izquierda alternativa exige imitar las medidas radicales sobre vivienda de Die Linke tras su éxito en Berlín
items.description: No es usual que el avispero de fuerzas a la izquierda del PSOE encuentre en la política europea asideros para reivindicarse como alternativa al auge de la extrema derecha. Este domingo sí le deparó uno. El éxito de Die Linke (La Izquierda) en las elecciones regionales de Berlín —donde su candidata, la germano-turca Elif Eralp , ha sido la más votada— ha desatado un aluvión de valoraciones en el espacio de la izquierda alternativa. Y ha prevalecido una interpretación: el triunfo de Eralp, con un programa centrado en la vivienda y la asequibilidad de los productos básicos —al estilo del alcalde socialista de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani —, debe marcar el camino hacia 2027, año en el que habrá elecciones autonómicas, municipales y previsiblemente generales. items.title: Acquisition of 12 AH-1Z viper attack helicopters major milestone — Army chief
items.description: The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Marshal Sunday Aneke, says the acquisition of 12 AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters for the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) is a major milestone. Aneke said this when he led the NAF delegation to Bell Textron in Amarillo, Texas, United States, for the beam signing ceremony. This is contained in a statement on Monday in Abuja, by the Director of Public Relations and Information, NAF Headquarters, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame. Aneke said the milestone represented an important step in the implementation of the Nigeria–United States Government defence cooperation programme and Nigeria’s ongoing efforts to modernise its armed forces. He also said that the acquisition reflected the strategic vision of the Federal Government of Nigeria to strengthen the nation’s defence and security architecture as well as provided the armed forces with requisite platforms and capabilities to address current and emerging security threats. The CAS expressed appreciation to President Bola Tinubu for his strategic leadership, unwavering support and commitment to strengthening the nation’s defence and security architecture. According to him, the acquisition demonstrates the federal government commitment to enhancing operational effectiveness of the Nigerian Armed Forces and ensuring that NAF remains adequately positioned to fulfil its constitutional responsibilities. “The acquisition of the AH-1Z Viper helicopters represents an important milestone in our continuing efforts to build a more capable, professional and mission-ready Nigerian Air Force.” The CAS also said that the acquisition aligned with his command philosophy of enhancing and sustaining highly motivated, professional and mission-ready force capable of delivering decisive airpower effects in synergy with surface forces to realise national security objectives. He stressed the need for personnel to ensure that the capabilities being acquired translate into enhanced operational effectiveness in support of national security. Aneke also acknowledged continued support and cooperation of the United States Government, Bell Textron, Programme Management of Air 276 and other stakeholders involved in the AH-1Z Viper programme. He emphasised that sustained defence cooperation, technical collaboration and capability development remained essential to successful implementation of the programme. ( NAN ) The post Acquisition of 12 AH-1Z viper attack helicopters major milestone — Army chief appeared first on Vanguard News .
